qs.p: The editor's comments on the draft were brief but ______: in a single sentence, she identified the flawed assumption that undermined the entire essay.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Comments that pinpoint the essay's central flaw in one sentence are sharp and penetrating: "incisive." "Rambling" contradicts "brief," "tentative" contradicts the decisive identification, and nothing suggests the comments were "flattering."

qs.p: The two teams' findings were strikingly ______: working independently on different continents, the researchers reached nearly identical conclusions about the virus's origin.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Findings that reached "nearly identical conclusions" are in agreement: "concordant." "Contradictory" is the opposite. "Preliminary" says nothing about agreement, and "derivative" (copied) conflicts with the teams' working independently.

qs.p: Rather than relying on a single narrator, the novel ______ its story among a dozen characters, each of whom describes only a small part of the events.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Giving each of a dozen characters part of the story spreads it among them: the novel "distributes" it. "Conceals" and "abandons" contradict the fact that the story is told, and dividing it among many voices doesn't "simplify" it.

qs.p: The following text is adapted from a short story.The sand on the island's eastern beach was so fine that it slipped through Amara's fingers like water, leaving only a pale dust on her palms.
qs.q: As used in the text, what does the word "fine" most nearly mean?
qs.e: Sand that slips through fingers like water and leaves dust is made of very small grains: "fine" here means powdery. "Excellent," "satisfactory," and "elegant" are other senses of "fine" that describe quality, not texture.

qs.p: The mountain's weather is notoriously ______: clear skies can give way to a blizzard within an hour, and climbers are warned to carry winter gear even in midsummer.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Weather that can change from clear skies to a blizzard within an hour is unpredictable and changeable: "capricious." "Predictable" and "monotonous" are the opposite, and "temperate" (mild) contradicts the danger described.

qs.p: Before the 1790s, units of measurement in France varied from town to town, which made trade and taxation confusing. The revolutionary government introduced a new unit, the meter, defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator along a line passing through Paris. Supporters argued that a unit based on Earth itself would belong to no single nation and could therefore be adopted by all.
qs.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To describe how surveyors measured the distance from the North Pole to the equator
To argue that the meter is more accurate than other units of length
To explain the reasoning behind the creation of a new unit of measurement
To criticize the variety of units used in France before the 1790s
qs.e: The text describes the problem (inconsistent local units), the new unit, and the argument for basing it on Earth. It doesn't claim the meter is more accurate, doesn't describe the surveying process, and presents the old system's confusion as background rather than as the focus of criticism.

qs.p: The following text is adapted from a novel.Nikolai arrived at the station an hour early, as he always did. He had missed a train once, in 1957, and had never quite forgiven himself. Now he sat on the bench with his ticket in his hand, glancing up at the clock every few minutes.
qs.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It explains the reason behind the character's habit of arriving early.
It describes where the character is traveling.
It reveals that the character dislikes traveling by train.
It suggests that the character will miss his train again.
qs.e: The underlined sentence gives the past event that explains why Nikolai "always" arrives an hour early and keeps checking the clock. It says nothing about his destination, gives no sign he will miss this train, and doesn't suggest he dislikes trains.

qs.p: Text 1Sharks have long been described as solitary animals that interact with one another mainly to mate or to compete for food.Text 2Biologist Yuki Mori fitted dozens of reef sharks with acoustic tags and tracked them for four years. She found that individual sharks repeatedly gathered with the same companions, forming stable social groups that persisted across seasons, even at times and places where no food was present.
qs.q: Based on the texts, how would Mori (Text 2) most likely respond to the description of sharks in Text 1?
c: She would argue that sharks never compete with one another for food.
She would argue that at least some sharks form lasting social bonds, contrary to the view that they are mainly solitary.
She would claim that all shark species live in permanent social groups.
She would agree that sharks gather only when competing for food.
qs.e: Mori found stable groups of the same companions that gathered even without food, which contradicts the solitary description. She doesn't agree that sharks gather only for food, says nothing denying competition, and studied reef sharks, so "all shark species" overgeneralizes.

qs.p: The following text is from Mark Twain's 1884 novel Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. The narrator is Huck Finn.You don't know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain't no matter. That book was made by Mr. Mark Twain, and he told the truth, mainly.
qs.q: Based on the text, how does the narrator characterize Mr. Mark Twain's earlier book?
c: As a completely invented story with no basis in fact
As mostly accurate, though not entirely truthful
As a book that readers must read before understanding the narrator
As a more truthful account than the narrator's own story
qs.e: "He told the truth, mainly" means mostly but not completely truthful. The narrator doesn't call it invented, says that not having read it "ain't no matter," and makes no comparison with his own story's truthfulness.

qs.p: Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that were still edible after thousands of years. Honey resists spoilage because it contains very little water and is acidic, conditions in which most bacteria and fungi cannot grow. In addition, an enzyme that bees add to nectar produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide, which further inhibits microbes.
qs.q: According to the text, which is one reason that honey resists spoilage?
c: It is kept at low temperatures.
It is stored in sealed pots.
qs.e: The text lists low water content, acidity, and hydrogen peroxide from an enzyme. Sealed pots and low temperatures aren't mentioned, and the text says honey does contain an enzyme.

qs.p: Linguist Omar Haddad hypothesizes that young children learn new words more effectively when the words appear in a story than when they are presented in a list.
qs.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haddad's hypothesis?
c: Children who studied word lists finished the activity more quickly than children who listened to stories.
Children said they enjoyed listening to stories more than studying word lists.
Children who heard ten new words in a story recalled more of them a week later than children who studied the same words in a list for the same amount of time.
Children who already knew many words learned new words faster than children who knew fewer words.
qs.e: The hypothesis compares learning in two formats. The finding in choice C compares retention of the same words after equal time in each format and favors stories. Enjoyment and speed don't measure learning, and the finding in choice D concerns prior vocabulary rather than format.

qs.p: In Langston Hughes's 1923 poem "Dreams," the speaker compares a life without dreams to something that has lost the ability to rise or move freely.
qs.q: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim?
c: "Life is a barren field / Frozen with snow."
"Life is a broken-winged bird / That cannot fly."
qs.e: The claim focuses on losing the ability to rise or move freely. A "broken-winged bird / That cannot fly" fits exactly. The "barren field / Frozen with snow" also describes a life without dreams, but it suggests emptiness and lack of growth, not lost movement. The other lines are the speaker's advice and a transition without a comparison.

qs.p:
Rainfall and Wheat Yield in Four Regions
RegionAverage annual rainfall (mm)Wheat yield (tonnes per hectare)
A6503.1
B5202.8
C4802.4
D3003.6
An agricultural economist notes that Region D, where farmers rely heavily on irrigation, achieved the highest wheat yield of the four regions despite receiving the least rainfall.
qs.q: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the economist's statement?
c: Region D received only 300 millimeters of rain, less than any other region, yet produced 3.6 tonnes of wheat per hectare, more than any other region.
Region C produced 2.4 tonnes of wheat per hectare.
Regions B and C received similar amounts of rainfall.
Region A received the most rainfall of the four regions.
qs.e: The statement has two parts: Region D had the least rain and the highest yield. Only choice A gives both, with comparisons to the other regions. The other choices describe other regions and don't address Region D.

qs.p: Young sunflowers track the sun across the sky each day, but mature sunflower heads stop moving and face east permanently. Researchers found that east-facing flower heads warmed up faster in the morning sun than flower heads that had been turned to face west, and that the east-facing flowers received far more visits from bees and other pollinators. These findings suggest that ______
qs.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: west-facing sunflowers receive more sunlight over the course of a day.
pollinators are unable to find sunflowers that face west.
facing east may benefit mature sunflowers by making them more attractive to pollinators.
young sunflowers track the sun in order to avoid pollinators.
qs.e: East-facing heads warmed faster and attracted more pollinators, which suggests a benefit to facing east. Nothing connects young sunflowers' tracking to avoiding pollinators, sunlight totals aren't compared, and west-facing flowers received fewer visits, not none.

qs.p: A sixteenth-century map of a stretch of coastline shows a river that appears on no modern map. Historians had assumed the river was an error or an invention of the mapmaker. Geologists studying the area, however, found sediment deposits showing that a river did flow at that location until it dried up around 1700. This finding suggests that ______
qs.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: modern maps of the coastline are inaccurate.
the mapmaker probably recorded a feature that actually existed at the time.
the river dried up before the map was made.
the mapmaker invented the river to make the map more interesting.
qs.e: The river existed until about 1700, long after the sixteenth-century map was made, so the mapmaker was likely recording a real feature. That contradicts the idea of invention; modern maps correctly omit a river that no longer exists; and the river dried up after, not before, the map was drawn.

qs.p: Giant sequoias can live for more than 3,000 ______ some living trees sprouted long before the founding of the Roman Empire.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: Both parts are independent clauses, so a semicolon is needed between them. A comma alone creates a comma splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and "which" makes the second clause ungrammatical.

qs.p: Neither the twins nor their older brother ______ ever seen the ocean, so the family's trip to the coast was a long-awaited event.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: With "neither … nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject. The nearer subject is "brother," which is singular, so "has" is correct.

qs.p: The city's two newest parks are very popular, but on weekends ______ playgrounds are often too crowded for younger children.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: The playgrounds belong to the two parks, a plural antecedent, so the plural possessive "their" is needed. "Its" is singular, "there" refers to a place, and "they're" means "they are."

qs.p: Last year, the observatory's survey telescope ______ more than 200 previously unknown asteroids.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: "Last year" refers to a finished period in the past, which calls for the simple past "discovered." The present perfect can't be used with a specific finished time like "last year," and the present and future tenses don't fit.

qs.p: In the dense rainforests of the Congo ______ researchers have used camera traps to record animals that are rarely seen by people.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: "In the dense rainforests of the Congo Basin" is a long introductory phrase, and a comma separates it from the main clause. A semicolon or colon would require an independent clause before it, and no punctuation makes the sentence hard to read.

qs.p: Located just south of the equator, ______
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: the city of Nairobi nonetheless has a mild climate because of its high elevation.
residents of Nairobi enjoy a mild climate because of the city's high elevation.
the high elevation of Nairobi gives the city a mild climate.
Nairobi's mild climate results from the city's high elevation.
qs.e: The opening phrase describes something located just south of the equator, so that thing, the city, must come right after the comma. A climate, an elevation, and residents are not what is "located just south of the equator."

qs.p: Most stars, including the Sun, shine with nearly constant brightness. ______ variable stars brighten and dim over periods ranging from a few hours to several years.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
qs.e: Variable stars differ from the steady stars described first, so "In contrast" fits. "Therefore" implies cause, "For example" would make variable stars an example of steady ones, and "Additionally" signals a similar point.

qs.p: To reduce food waste, the school cafeteria began composting leftover food and donating unopened items to a local shelter. ______ it now sends only about half as much trash to the landfill as it did before.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
qs.e: Sending less trash to the landfill is the outcome of composting and donating, so "As a result" fits. "However" and "Instead" signal contrast or replacement, and "Similarly" signals a parallel point.

qs.p: Educated people in ancient Greece knew that Earth was round. ______ around 240 BCE, the scholar Eratosthenes estimated Earth's circumference by comparing the angles of the sun's rays at two Egyptian cities.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
qs.e: The second sentence goes further than the first: Greeks not only knew Earth was round but estimated its size. "In fact" introduces such an intensifying point. "Nevertheless" and "Instead" signal contrast, and "Meanwhile" signals simultaneous but separate events.

qs.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The International Space Station orbits about 400 kilometers above Earth.
  • It travels at roughly 28,000 kilometers per hour.
  • It completes one orbit around Earth about every 90 minutes.
  • As a result, astronauts aboard see about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day.
qs.q: The student wants to emphasize how often astronauts on the station see the sun rise. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The International Space Station orbits about 400 kilometers above Earth.
The International Space Station completes one orbit around Earth about every 90 minutes.
Because the International Space Station orbits Earth about every 90 minutes, astronauts aboard it see about 16 sunrises each day.
The International Space Station travels at roughly 28,000 kilometers per hour.
qs.e: Only choice C states how many sunrises astronauts see and why. The others give the station's altitude, speed, or orbital period without mentioning sunrises.

qs.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The Tale of Genji was written by Murasaki Shikibu in Japan in the early eleventh century.
  • It is sometimes called the world's first novel.
  • Don Quixote was written by Miguel de Cervantes in Spain.
  • It was published in two parts, in 1605 and 1615.
  • It is often called the first modern European novel.
qs.q: The student wants to emphasize how much earlier The Tale of Genji was written than Don Quixote. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Don Quixote was published in two parts, in 1605 and 1615.
The Tale of Genji is sometimes called the world's first novel.
Don Quixote, by Miguel de Cervantes, is often called the first modern European novel.
Murasaki Shikibu's The Tale of Genji, written in the early eleventh century, predates Cervantes's Don Quixote, published in 1605 and 1615, by roughly six hundred years.
qs.e: Only choice D gives both dates and states the size of the gap. The others describe one work each without comparing when they were written.

qs.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The Terracotta Army is a collection of thousands of life-size clay soldiers.
  • It was buried with Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China, who died in 210 BCE.
  • In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an, China, uncovered fragments of the figures.
  • Archaeologists have since excavated about 2,000 of an estimated 8,000 soldiers.
qs.q: The student wants to describe how the Terracotta Army was discovered. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The Terracotta Army consists of thousands of life-size clay soldiers.
Archaeologists have excavated about 2,000 of an estimated 8,000 terracotta soldiers.
The Terracotta Army was discovered in 1974, when farmers digging a well near Xi'an, China, uncovered fragments of the clay figures.
The Terracotta Army was buried with Qin Shi Huang, who died in 210 BCE.
qs.e: Only choice C explains how the discovery happened (farmers digging a well in 1974). The others describe the army's origin, the progress of excavation, or what the army is.

qs.p: The ambassador was admired for her ______: she could express firm disagreement while still leaving her counterparts feeling respected.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Disagreeing firmly without giving offense is the definition of "tact." "Bluntness" would not leave counterparts feeling respected, "indecision" contradicts "firm disagreement," and "bravado" (showy boldness) doesn't fit.

qs.p: The authors' sweeping conclusions were not ______ by their data: the improvements they cited all fell within the study's margin of error.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Improvements within the margin of error don't justify sweeping conclusions, so the conclusions were not "warranted" by the data. "Not contradicted" would mean the data were consistent with the conclusions, the opposite point. "Anticipated" and "obscured" don't describe how data relate to conclusions.

qs.p: The senator's support for the bill was ______ at best: she voted for it but declined to speak in its favor and privately expressed doubts about its effectiveness.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Voting for a bill while refusing to speak for it and privately doubting it shows weak, reluctant support: "halfhearted." "Unwavering" and "vociferous" (loud, insistent) describe strong support, and "unprecedented" doesn't describe the strength of support.

qs.p: The following text is adapted from a history of a museum.For three decades the museum's founder exercised considerable influence over which artists were shown, and few exhibitions opened without her approval.
qs.q: As used in the text, what does the word "exercised" most nearly mean?
qs.e: To exercise influence is to use or wield it, as shown by exhibitions needing her approval. "Practiced" (rehearsed) and "trained" relate to physical or skill-building exercise, and "worried" reflects the sense of being "exercised about" something.

qs.p: The novelist's portrayal of the small town is ______: she depicts its residents' generosity and pettiness, courage and hypocrisy, without excusing or condemning any of them.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Showing both virtues and flaws without excusing or condemning is a complex, balanced portrayal: "nuanced." "Idealized" would show only virtues, "scathing" only flaws, and "cursory" (superficial) contradicts the detailed range described.

qs.p: Psychologists once believed that infants are born unable to perceive depth and learn to do so only after they begin to crawl. In the "visual cliff" experiments of the 1960s, however, crawling infants refused to move onto a sheet of glass placed over an apparent drop. Later studies found that even infants too young to crawl showed changes in heart rate when placed above the drop, suggesting that they perceived it, though their fear of heights appeared to develop only after they began crawling.
qs.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To show that infants are born with a fear of heights
To explain how the glass in the visual cliff experiments was constructed
To describe how research changed scientists' understanding of when a perceptual ability develops
To argue that infants should not be allowed to crawl until they can perceive depth
qs.e: The text traces a shift from the belief that depth perception follows crawling to evidence that it appears earlier. It makes no recommendation, doesn't describe the apparatus in detail, and says fear of heights seems to develop only after crawling, not at birth.

qs.p: The ancient Greek historian Herodotus described "gold-digging ants" in a region east of Persia: fox-sized creatures that dug up gold-rich sand. For centuries, readers dismissed the story as fantasy. <u>In 1996, however, French explorer Michel Peissel reported that on a high plateau in northern Pakistan, marmots dig burrows in gold-bearing sand, and local people have traditionally collected the gold dust from the soil the animals excavate.</u> Peissel suggested that Herodotus's account was a distorted report of this practice.
qs.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It explains why readers dismissed Herodotus's account for centuries.
It presents a modern observation that suggests a possible factual basis for an account long considered fiction.
It provides evidence that Herodotus personally visited northern Pakistan.
It describes a method that Herodotus recommended for collecting gold.
qs.e: The underlined sentence reports Peissel's observation of gold-digging marmots, which, according to the next sentence, may explain Herodotus's "fantasy." It doesn't show Herodotus visited the region, the reason for past dismissal is given in the previous sentence, and Herodotus didn't recommend a method.

qs.p: Text 1Some historians describe the centuries after the fall of the Western Roman Empire as the "Dark Ages," a period of cultural and intellectual decline in Western Europe.Text 2Historian Ingrid Solberg contends that this label reflects what has survived more than what was produced. Many works from the period were written on perishable materials or kept in monastic libraries that were later destroyed, and scholarship flourished in centers such as Ireland and Northumbria. The period seems "dark," Solberg argues, partly because historians have less evidence about it, not because less was happening.
qs.q: Based on the texts, how would Solberg (Text 2) most likely respond to the historians' description in Text 1?
c: She would argue that their impression of decline may be shaped by gaps in the surviving evidence.
She would argue that the Western Roman Empire never fell.
She would claim that more works survive from this period than from any other.
She would agree that little scholarship took place anywhere in Western Europe during the period.
qs.e: Solberg attributes the "dark" impression to lost evidence and points to flourishing scholarship, which challenges the idea of real decline. She explicitly denies that little scholarship occurred, doesn't dispute the empire's fall, and argues that relatively little survives.

qs.p: Music histories often describe the European symphony orchestra as having reached a standard form in the nineteenth century. Yet surviving rosters of orchestras from that period show wide variation: some ensembles had as few as twenty players and others more than a hundred, and the balance of string to wind instruments differed from city to city. Musicologist Alma Kessler argues that the "standard orchestra" is largely a twentieth-century idea projected back onto a far more varied past.
qs.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Kessler argues that twentieth-century orchestras are less varied than earlier ones.
Evidence from the period suggests that nineteenth-century orchestras were more varied than the idea of a "standard orchestra" implies.
Nineteenth-century orchestras always had more than a hundred players.
String instruments were rarely used in nineteenth-century orchestras.
qs.e: The text sets a common claim (a standard form) against roster evidence of wide variation and presents Kessler's conclusion that the standard is a later idea. Sizes ranged from twenty to over a hundred, Kessler doesn't compare twentieth-century variety, and the text discusses the balance of strings and winds, not an absence of strings.

qs.p: The following text is adapted from a novel.When the new teacher asked the class to write about a person they admired, most of the children chose athletes or film stars. Eli wrote about the man who drove the morning bus, who greeted every child by name and who had once waited ten minutes in the snow while Eli ran home for a forgotten mitten. The teacher read the essay twice and then, without a word, pinned it to the wall.
qs.q: Based on the text, what does the teacher's action most likely suggest?
c: She pinned every student's essay to the wall.
She wanted the bus driver to read Eli's essay.
She disapproved of Eli's choice of subject.
She was moved by Eli's essay and wanted to recognize it.
qs.e: Reading the essay twice and then displaying it singles it out, suggesting she valued it. Displaying work signals approval, not disapproval; the text says nothing about other essays being pinned up; and nothing connects her action to the bus driver reading it.

qs.p: Lexicographer Tomas Reyes claims that the English word "cookie" entered the language in North America during the seventeenth or eighteenth century, borrowed from koekje, the Dutch word for a small cake, which Dutch settlers in New York used.
qs.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Reyes's claim?
c: The word koekje is still used in the Netherlands today.
Many other English words, such as "boss" and "sleigh," were borrowed from Dutch in New York.
A cookbook printed in London in 1550 uses the word "cookie" to refer to a small cake.
Dutch settlers in New York baked many kinds of small cakes.
qs.e: If "cookie" appeared in a London book in 1550, the word existed in English before Dutch settlers arrived in New York, which undercuts the claimed origin. The other findings are consistent with Reyes's claim and would, if anything, support it.

qs.p: A transportation researcher claims that public transit was the most common way to commute in the large city but that driving was the most common way to commute in both of the other places surveyed.
qs.q: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the researcher's claim?
c: Only 5% of workers in the small town commuted by public transit.
In both the mid-sized city and the small town, 15% of workers walked or biked to work.
In the large city, 45% of workers commuted by public transit, more than by any other mode, while in the mid-sized city and the small town, driving was the most common mode, at 65% and 80%.
The share of workers commuting by car rose from 35% in the large city to 80% in the small town, while the share commuting by public transit fell from 45% to 5%.
qs.e: The claim requires identifying the most common mode in each of the three places. Choice C does: transit leads in the large city, driving in the other two. The other choices describe one trend or one value and don't establish which mode was most common in each place.

qs.p: In William Shakespeare's play Hamlet, first performed around 1600, the title character considers whether it is nobler to endure suffering patiently or to fight against it.
qs.q: Which quotation from Hamlet most effectively illustrates the claim?
c: "Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer / The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, / Or to take arms against a sea of troubles / And by opposing end them."
"To be, or not to be, that is the question:"
qs.e: The claim is a comparison between enduring and resisting suffering, judged by nobility. Only choice B states both options ("to suffer" or "to take arms") and asks which is "nobler." The famous opening line poses a question without naming the two options, and the other lines move on to death and its uncertainty.

qs.p: The flowers of many plants open and close at particular times of day. In an experiment, researchers placed one such plant in a greenhouse kept under constant light and temperature, with no day or night. For several days, the plant's flowers continued to open and close on a cycle of roughly 24 hours. These results suggest that ______
qs.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: the plant cannot survive without regular periods of darkness.
the flowers open only in response to increasing light in the morning.
constant light causes flowers to stop opening and closing.
the timing of the flowers' opening is controlled at least partly by an internal rhythm rather than only by daily changes in light.
qs.e: With no day-night cues, the flowers still kept a roughly 24-hour cycle, so something internal must keep time. That contradicts the idea that they respond only to light; nothing in the experiment addresses survival; and the flowers kept opening and closing under constant light.

qs.p: At an ancient settlement site in Peru, archaeologists found many charred maize cobs. Chemical analysis of human bones from the same period at the site, however, showed little of the distinctive carbon signature that a diet rich in maize leaves in human tissue. These findings suggest that ______
qs.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: the residents of the site did not know how to grow maize.
although maize was present at the site, it may not have been a major part of most residents' diets.
maize was the main food eaten by the site's residents.
the maize cobs found at the site were brought there in modern times.
qs.e: Maize was clearly present (charred cobs), but bones lack the signature of heavy maize eating, so it likely wasn't a dietary staple. The cobs show maize was there, nothing suggests they're modern, and the bone evidence contradicts maize as the main food.

qs.p: The term "Anthropocene," which some scientists have proposed as the name for the current geological ______ emphasizes humanity's profound influence on Earth's climate, oceans, and ecosystems.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: The clause "which some scientists have proposed …" opens with a comma after "Anthropocene," so it must close with a comma before the verb "emphasizes." No punctuation leaves it unclosed, a semicolon would split the subject from its verb, and a dash can't close a clause opened by a comma.

qs.p: A number of researchers ______ questioned whether the study's sample was large enough to support its conclusions.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb: "A number of researchers have." (By contrast, "the number of" refers to a single quantity and takes a singular verb.)

qs.p: The emergency kit includes several essential ______ a compass, a whistle, a signal mirror, and a waterproof flashlight.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: "The emergency kit includes several essential tools" is a complete clause, and a colon introduces the list that specifies them. A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, and a colon never follows "such as," which already introduces the examples.

qs.p: For the past decade, engineers at the laboratory ______ new ways to store solar energy for use at night.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: "For the past decade" describes an activity that began in the past and continues to the present, which calls for the present perfect progressive: "have been developing." "Had been developing" requires a later past reference point, and "will develop" and "developed" don't fit an ongoing activity.

qs.p: The prize committee praised the novel's inventive ______ its plot, which several judges found predictable.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: A contrasting element introduced by "not" is set off with a comma: "praised the novel's inventive structure, not its plot." A comma after "not" breaks the phrase, and a semicolon or colon requires an independent clause after it.

qs.p: Before the museum's new wing opened, each tool and each scientific instrument in the collection ______ cleaned, photographed, and catalogued.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: When "each" introduces nouns joined by "and," the subject is treated as singular, so the singular verb "was" is required. The past tense also fits "before the … wing opened."

qs.p: Some critics have argued that the composer's late works show a decline in creativity. ______ others regard them as her most daring compositions, pointing to their unusual harmonies and fragmented forms.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
qs.e: The second sentence presents the opposite view of the same works, so "Conversely" fits. "Thus" implies a consequence, "Specifically" introduces detail, and "Likewise" signals agreement.

qs.p: Instruments aboard a rover detected methane in the atmosphere of Mars. ______ methane can be produced both by living organisms and by geological processes, so its presence alone does not indicate that life exists there.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
qs.e: The second sentence qualifies the excitement of the detection by noting a non-biological explanation, which contrasts with any assumption that methane means life. "However" signals that. "Therefore" implies a consequence, and "Similarly" and "For example" don't introduce a qualification.

qs.p: Many cosmologists in the 1990s expected that gravity was gradually slowing the expansion of the universe. ______ observations of distant exploding stars in 1998 showed that the expansion is actually speeding up.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
qs.e: The 1998 observations contradicted what cosmologists expected, so "Surprisingly" fits. "Accordingly" implies the result matched expectations, "Likewise" signals similarity, and "In other words" signals restatement.

qs.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Cahokia was a city built by the Mississippian culture near present-day St. Louis.
  • Around 1100 CE, it may have had 10,000 to 20,000 residents.
  • That made it the largest settlement in North America north of Mexico at the time.
  • Its largest earthwork, Monks Mound, covers about 6 hectares at its base.
qs.q: The student wants to emphasize the size of Cahokia's population. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Cahokia was a city built by the Mississippian culture near present-day St. Louis.
Cahokia was located near present-day St. Louis.
Cahokia's largest earthwork, Monks Mound, covers about 6 hectares at its base.
Around 1100 CE, Cahokia may have had 10,000 to 20,000 residents, making it the largest settlement in North America north of Mexico at the time.
qs.e: Only choice D gives Cahokia's population and its significance. The others describe its builders, location, or largest earthwork.

qs.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Architects and planners use several approaches to caring for historic buildings.
  • Restoration returns a building to its appearance at a particular moment in its history, removing later additions.
  • Preservation maintains a building as it currently exists, including changes made over time.
  • Both approaches aim to protect a building's historic character.
qs.q: The student wants to contrast restoration and preservation. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Restoration returns a building to its appearance at a particular moment in its history.
Architects and planners use several approaches to caring for historic buildings.
Whereas restoration returns a historic building to how it looked at a particular moment, preservation maintains it as it currently exists, including later changes.
Both restoration and preservation aim to protect a building's historic character.
qs.e: Only choice C describes both approaches and sets them against each other. Choice D states a similarity, choice A describes one approach, and choice B is a general statement.

qs.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The volcano Krakatoa, in present-day Indonesia, erupted in August 1883.
  • The eruption's pressure waves circled the globe several times.
  • The sound was heard on Rodrigues Island in the Indian Ocean, nearly 4,800 kilometers away.
  • It is often described as the loudest sound in recorded history.
qs.q: The student wants to emphasize how far the sound of the eruption traveled. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Krakatoa, in present-day Indonesia, erupted in August 1883.
The eruption of Krakatoa is often described as the loudest sound in recorded history.
The sound of Krakatoa's 1883 eruption was heard on Rodrigues Island, nearly 4,800 kilometers away.
The pressure waves from Krakatoa's eruption circled the globe several times.
qs.e: Only choice C states how far away the sound was heard. The others give the date, a general description, or the pressure waves (which traveled far but weren't heard as sound everywhere).

qs.q: If 8 − 3x = 2x − 12, what is the value of x?
qs.e: Add 3x and 12 to both sides: 20 = 5x, so x = 4. (20 is the value of 5x.)

qs.q: A pool is being drained. The amount of water W, in gallons, remaining in the pool t minutes after draining begins is modeled by W = 18,000 − 600t. What is the best interpretation of 18,000 in this context?
c: The number of gallons drained each minute
The number of minutes needed to drain the pool
The number of gallons remaining after one minute
The number of gallons in the pool when draining begins
qs.e: When t = 0, W = 18,000, so 18,000 is the amount of water at the start. The 600 is the gallons drained per minute, and the pool empties after 18,000 ÷ 600 = 30 minutes.

qs.q: A cyclist rides 27 kilometers in 1.5 hours. At this rate, how many kilometers will the cyclist ride in 40 minutes?
qs.e: The cyclist's rate is 27 ÷ 1.5 = 18 kilometers per hour. Forty minutes is 2/3 of an hour, so the distance is 18 × 2/3 = 12 kilometers.

qs.q: Which expression is equivalent to (4x2)(3x3)?
qs.e: Multiply the coefficients (4 × 3 = 12) and add the exponents of x (2 + 3 = 5): 12x5. Adding the coefficients or multiplying the exponents are common errors.

qs.q:
Prefers dogsPrefers cats
Grade 112812
Grade 122218
The table shows the pet preferences of 80 students. What percent of the students who prefer cats are in grade 11?
qs.e: 30 students prefer cats (12 + 18), and 12 of them are in grade 11: 12/30 = 40%. (30% is the share of grade 11 students who prefer cats, 12/40, which answers a different question.)

qs.q: The function f is defined by f(x) = 3x2 − 5. What is the value of f(−3)?
qs.e: f(−3) = 3(−3)2 − 5 = 3(9) − 5 = 22. Squaring −3 gives positive 9.

qs.q: In the xy-plane, the line y = mx + 4 is perpendicular to the line y = −12x + 1. What is the value of m?
qs.e: Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1, so m × (−1/2) = −1 and m = 2. (−2 is the reciprocal without the sign change; −1/2 would make the lines parallel.)

qs.q: A rectangular tank measuring 2 meters by 1.5 meters by 0.8 meter is completely filled with water. The tank is drained at a constant rate of 12 liters per minute. How many minutes will it take to empty the tank? (1 cubic meter = 1,000 liters)
qs.e: The volume is 2 × 1.5 × 0.8 = 2.4 cubic meters, which is 2.4 × 1,000 = 2,400 liters. At 12 liters per minute, draining takes 2,400 ÷ 12 = 200 minutes. (2,400 is the volume in liters, not the time.)

qs.q: A data set of 7 values has a median of 15. If the largest value in the data set is doubled, what is the median of the new data set?
qs.e: The median of 7 values is the 4th value in order. Doubling the largest value makes it even larger, so it stays in 7th place and the 4th value doesn't change. The median remains 15.

qs.q: The measures of the angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. What is the measure of the largest angle?
qs.e: The angles are 2k, 3k, and 4k, and they sum to 180°: 9k = 180, so k = 20. The largest angle is 4(20) = 80°.

qs.q: What is the larger of the two solutions to the equation x2 − 9x + 20 = 0?
qs.e: Factor: (x − 4)(x − 5) = 0. The solutions are 4 and 5, and the larger is 5.

qs.q: The number of bacteria in a culture t hours after it is started is modeled by N(t) = 300(2)t. According to the model, after how many hours will the culture contain 4,800 bacteria?
qs.e: 300(2)t = 4,800, so 2t = 16 and t = 4. (16 is the value of 2t, not of t.)

qs.q: Which expression is equivalent to (x + 4)(x − 4) − (x − 4)2?
A bicycle wheel has a diameter of 70 centimeters. How far, in centimeters, does the bicycle travel when the wheel makes one complete revolution without slipping?
qs.e: In one revolution the bicycle travels a distance equal to the wheel's circumference: π × diameter = 70π centimeters (about 220 cm). (140π comes from using 2π times the diameter instead of 2π times the radius, 35.)

qs.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 34 centimeters and a diagonal of 13 centimeters. What is the area of the rectangle, in square centimeters?
qs.e: Let the sides be l and w: l + w = 17 and l2 + w2 = 169. Then (l + w)2 = 289 = 169 + 2lw, so 2lw = 120 and the area lw = 60. (The sides are 12 and 5.)

qs.q: The population of a city increased from 80,000 to 92,000. By what percent did the population increase?
qs.e: Percent increase = (92,000 − 80,000)/80,000 × 100 = 12,000/80,000 × 100 = 15%. Dividing by the new population (12,000/92,000 ≈ 13%) uses the wrong base.

qs.q: The cost, in dollars, of renting a van for x miles is y = 0.5x + 20 at Company A and y = 0.75x + 5 at Company B. The graphs of the two equations intersect at (60, 50). What does this point represent?
c: Company B is cheaper for every distance up to 60 miles.
Both companies charge $50 for a 60-mile rental.
qs.e: At the intersection both equations give the same y-value for the same x-value: at 60 miles, both cost $50. (Company B is actually cheaper below 60 miles, but the point itself represents equal cost, not a per-mile price.)

qs.q: For an acute angle θ, tan θ = 1. What is the value of sin θ?
qs.e: tan θ = 1 means the opposite and adjacent sides are equal, so θ = 45°. In a 45°-45°-90° triangle, sin 45° = √2/2.

qs.q: If 2x = 32, what is the value of 2x − 2?
qs.e: 2x − 2 = 2x ÷ 22 = 32 ÷ 4 = 8. (Alternatively, x = 5, so 23 = 8.)

qs.q: A cube has a volume of 64 cubic inches. What is the total surface area of the cube, in square inches?
qs.e: The edge length is ∛64 = 4. Each of the 6 faces has area 16, so the surface area is 6 × 16 = 96. (16 is the area of one face.)

qs.q: Which equation describes all numbers x on a number line that are exactly 3 units from 5?
qs.e: |x − 5| is the distance between x and 5, so the equation |x − 5| = 3 describes the points 2 and 8. |x + 5| = 3 describes points 3 units from −5.

qs.q: The digits of a two-digit number add up to 9. When the digits are reversed, the new number is 27 greater than the original number. What is the original number?
qs.e: Let the tens digit be a and the units digit b: a + b = 9 and (10b + a) − (10a + b) = 9(b − a) = 27, so b − a = 3. Then a = 3 and b = 6, so the number is 36. Check: 63 − 36 = 27.

qs.q:
5x + 2y = 20
y = 3x − 1
If (x, y) is the solution to the system of equations above, what is the value of x?
How many distinct real solutions does the equation x3 − 4x = 0 have?
qs.e: Factor: x(x2 − 4) = x(x − 2)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 0, 2, or −2: three distinct real solutions. Dividing both sides by x loses the solution x = 0.

qs.q: The function f is defined by f(x) = kx + 7, where k is a constant. If f(3) = 2f(1), what is the value of k?
In a club, the ratio of juniors to seniors is 3 : 5. After 12 more juniors join the club and no seniors join or leave, the ratio of juniors to seniors is 1 : 1. How many seniors are in the club?
qs.e: Let the original numbers be 3k juniors and 5k seniors. After 12 juniors join, 3k + 12 = 5k, so 2k = 12 and k = 6. There are 5(6) = 30 seniors (and 18 original juniors, which becomes 30 after 12 join).

qs.q: Triangle ABC is inscribed in a circle, and side AB is a diameter of the circle. If the measure of angle A is 35°, what is the measure of angle B?
qs.e: An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle, so angle C = 90°. Then angle B = 180° − 90° − 35° = 55°.

qs.q: A rectangle has an area of 54 square meters, and its length is 1.5 times its width. What is the perimeter of the rectangle, in meters?
qs.e: Let the width be w: 1.5w2 = 54, so w2 = 36 and w = 6. The length is 9, and the perimeter is 2(6 + 9) = 30.

qs.q: A quantity triples every 4 years. By approximately what factor does the quantity increase over 6 years?
qs.e: Six years is 6/4 = 1.5 tripling periods, so the factor is 31.5 = 3√3 ≈ 5.2. Multiplying 3 by 1.5 (4.5) treats exponential growth as linear.

qs.q: The graph of the linear function f in the xy-plane passes through the points (1, 3) and (4, 9). What is the x-coordinate of the x-intercept of the graph?
qs.e: The slope is (9 − 3)/(4 − 1) = 2, so f(x) = 2x + 1. Setting 2x + 1 = 0 gives x = −1/2.

qs.q: In a right triangle, angle A is acute and sin A = 35. What is the value of sin Acos A?
qs.e: With opposite side 3 and hypotenuse 5, the adjacent side is 4, so cos A = 4/5. Then sin A/cos A = (3/5)/(4/5) = 3/4, which is tan A.

qs.q: The data set 6, 9, 9, 11, x has a mean equal to its mode. If x is not equal to 9, what is the value of x?
qs.e: Since x ≠ 9, the mode is 9 (the only repeated value). A mean of 9 for 5 values requires a sum of 45: 6 + 9 + 9 + 11 + x = 35 + x = 45, so x = 10.

qs.q: Which of the following is a factor of 2x2 + 7x + 3?
qs.e: Factor: 2x2 + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3). Check: 2x2 + 6x + x + 3. So 2x + 1 is a factor.

qs.q: A store raised all of its prices by 25%. By what percent must the new prices be reduced to return them to their original values?
qs.e: The new price is 1.25 times the original. To return to the original, multiply by 1/1.25 = 0.80, a 20% reduction. A 25% cut would leave 0.75 × 1.25 = 0.9375 of the original.

qs.q: Two fair six-sided number cubes, each with faces numbered 1 through 6, are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers rolled is 8?
qs.e: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. A sum of 8 occurs for (2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 3), and (6, 2): 5 outcomes, so the probability is 5/36. (1/9 = 4/36 misses one of the five outcomes, often (4, 4); 1/6 = 6/36 is the probability of a sum of 7.)

qs.q: In the xy-plane, the circle x2 + y2 = 50 and the line y = x intersect at the point (a, a), where a > 0. What is the value of a?
qs.e: Substitute y = x: 2x2 = 50, so x2 = 25 and x = ±5. Since a > 0, a = 5.

qs.q: The function f is defined by f(x) = x2 − 4x. For what value of c does the equation f(x) = c have exactly one real solution?
qs.e: The graph of f is a parabola opening upward with vertex at x = 2, where f(2) = 4 − 8 = −4. A horizontal line y = c meets the parabola exactly once only at the vertex, so c = −4. (Equivalently, x2 − 4x − c = 0 has discriminant 16 + 4c, which is 0 when c = −4. With c = 0 there are two solutions, 0 and 4.)

qs.q: What is the area of an equilateral triangle with sides of length 10?
qs.e: The height of an equilateral triangle with side 10 is 5√3 (from a 30°-60°-90° triangle). Area = (1/2)(10)(5√3) = 25√3 ≈ 43.3. (50 uses the side, 10, as the height.)

qs.q: A line in the xy-plane passes through the points (0, k) and (4, 0) and has a slope of −32. What is the value of k?

y = x2 − 6x + 5
y = −x + 5
Which of the following ordered pairs (x, y) is a solution to the system of equations above?
qs.e: Set x2 − 6x + 5 = −x + 5, so x2 − 5x = 0 and x = 0 or 5. The solutions are (0, 5) and (5, 0). (1, 4) lies on the line but not the parabola, and (3, −4) is the parabola's vertex but not on the line.

qs.q: In a random sample of 150 of a school's 1,200 students, 36 said they walk to school. Based on the sample, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of students at the school who walk to school?
qs.e: The sample proportion is 36/150 = 0.24. Applied to all 1,200 students: 0.24 × 1,200 = 288.

qs.q: A triangle has sides of lengths 13, 14, and 15. What is the area of the triangle?
qs.e: Drop an altitude h to the side of length 14, dividing it into parts p and 14 − p. Then 132 − p2 = 152 − (14 − p)2, which gives p = 5 and h = √13² − 5² = 12. Area = (1/2)(14)(12) = 84.

qs.q: If (18)x = 4x + 5, what is the value of x?
qs.e: Write both sides with base 2: (2−3)x = (22)x + 5, so −3x = 2x + 10. Then −5x = 10 and x = −2.

qs.q: The function f is defined by f(x) = x2 + bx + c, where b and c are constants. If f(1) = f(5) and the minimum value of f is −4, what is the value of c?
qs.e: Since f(1) = f(5), the axis of symmetry is midway at x = 3, so −b/2 = 3 and b = −6. The minimum is f(3) = 9 − 18 + c = c − 9 = −4, so c = 5.
